Framework nine, Falsification Tests. These are related to placebo tests but more targeted. Instead of just checking whether an effect appears where it should not, you derive specific predictions from your causal model and check whether they hold. Your causal model is on trial, and you are the prosecutor.

In our ad example, suppose your DAG says the ad works through emotional arousal, not through providing new information. That gives you a testable prediction. Agents who see the ad but have emotional responses disabled in the simulation should show no change in voting intention. If they still shift, your mechanism is wrong. The overall effect might still be real, it might just work through a different pathway than you thought. The more falsification predictions your model survives, the stronger it gets. But no number of passed tests can prove the model is true. They only show it has not yet been refuted.

And finally, framework ten. DAG based Sensitivity Analysis. A DAG is a directed acyclic graph. It is a visual map of your causal assumptions, which variables cause which, and what you have and have not measured. DAG based sensitivity analysis uses this map to systematically identify which unobserved variables could bias your estimate, and by how much. The Cinelli and Hazlett framework is especially useful here. In our example, your DAG includes media diet, age, party affiliation, and ad exposure. But you suspect there is an unobserved variable, call it social media echo chamber intensity, that affects both ad exposure and voting intention. Using the Cinelli Hazlett method, you can calculate that this variable would need an R squared of 0.15 with both exposure and outcome to explain away the effect. If you believe that is implausibly high, your estimate survives. The limitation is obvious. The analysis is only as good as the DAG you draw. If you miss an important edge or get the direction wrong, the whole thing is undermined.
